title: Three Names on the Medal, Hundreds in the Record
source_status: Original adaptation of film catalogue premise and documented Nobel Foundation/CERN/Science History Institute primary records; full original Substack essay unavailable

scenes.text: A medal creates a beautiful image of discovery: one name, perhaps two, sometimes three. The experiment behind it rarely fits inside the frame.
The Nobel Foundation's statutes set a firm boundary: no prize amount may be divided among more than three people. That is an award rule, not a map of every contribution.
Scientific discoveries move through generations of instruments, questions, negative results, corrections, and people who make the decisive experiment possible.
Consider the structure of DNA. In nineteen fifty-two, Rosalind Franklin and her student Raymond Gosling produced the X-ray diffraction evidence known as Photograph Fifty-One.
The nineteen sixty-two medicine prize went to Watson, Crick and Wilkins. Franklin had died in nineteen fifty-eight. The historical argument over credit is real, but her contribution is documented.
Now consider a different discovery. In nineteen sixty-four, Brout and Englert, and independently Higgs, proposed a mechanism connected to the origin of elementary-particle mass.
In July twenty twelve, the ATLAS and CMS collaborations announced a new particle consistent with the Higgs boson. Each collaboration involved more than three thousand people.
One year later, the physics Nobel honored François Englert and Peter Higgs for the theoretical mechanism, experimentally confirmed at CERN. The award had a specific subject.
That distinction matters. Recognizing a theory is not the same as crediting every detector engineer, software specialist, student, technician, and analyst who made its test possible.
A prize does not invent these missing contributions. But a historian must not invent them either. Attribution begins with papers, laboratory records, archival correspondence, and documented roles.
The public ceremony compresses a scientific genealogy into a few recognizable names. It can celebrate a genuine achievement without telling the complete story of its making.
We do not need fewer prizes. We need histories capacious enough to follow the work beyond the stage, and give evidence-based credit where the record allows it.
